title: Comprehensive Visible and Near-infrared Keck and Gemini Monitoring and Characterization of Interstellar Comet 3I/ATLAS during its Encounter with the Solar System
summary: We present 14 optical imaging and eight optical spectroscopic epochs of interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS from Keck/LRIS and Gemini/GMOS, two near-infrared (NIR) imaging epochs from Keck/MOSFIRE, and four NIR spectroscopic epochs from Gemini/Flamingos-2 and GNIRS, obtained between 2025 July and 2026 May. Mean GMOS colors of $g-r=0.732\pm0.029$, $r-i=0.237\pm0.025$, and $i-z=0.109\pm0.022$ mag show no significant change across perihelion. Phase-corrected red-band activity follows $Afρ\propto r_h^{-2.10\pm0.14}$ inbound and $r_h^{-3.34\pm0.43}$ outbound. Transverse-width and sunward-plume speeds imply dust losses of $2.7\times10^9$ and $1.0\times10^{10}$ kg over 2025 July 3--2026 May 15 for 1-$μ$m--1-mm grains, equivalent to global layers of 0.26 and 0.99 m under the adopted grain and nucleus assumptions. The concentrated coma, compact sunward feature, and antisolar tail seen on 2025 August 27 broadened by 2025 November 26; extended dust persisted through 2026 February 17. C$_2$/CN nearly doubled from $0.257\pm0.014$ on 2025 September 14--15 to $0.481\pm0.080$ on 2025 November 26, while C$_3$/CN fell from $0.327\pm0.024$ on 2025 August 28 to $0.214\pm0.009$ on 2025 September 14--15. MOSFIRE NIR imaging on 2025 July 11 gives $Y-J=0.466\pm0.143$, $J-H=0.239\pm0.052$, $H-K_s=0.454\pm0.150$, and $J-K_s=0.693\pm0.202$ mag. Spectra give $J-H=0.24$ mag on 2025 September 5--6 and $J-H=0.27$--0.28 and $J-K_s=0.21$--0.22 mag on 2025 December 1--2 over the retained passband intervals. Model-calibrated imaging on 2026 February 6 gives near-solar $J-K_s=0.303\pm0.051$ mag. No water-ice absorption is robust to the tested continuum and calibration choices in the NIR spectra. These observations provide a lasting record of the comet's evolution through the Solar System and a benchmark for studying and monitoring future interstellar objects.

title: A Population Synthesis Model for Odd Radio Circles Produced by Shock-Bubble Interactions
summary: Odd Radio Circles (ORCs) are edge-brightened rings of diffuse radio emission of roughly arcminute size whose physical origin remains debated. One proposed mechanism is vortex formation through Shock-Bubble interaction (SBI), in which a merger or accretion shock re-energizes a fossil radio lobe into an edge-brightened ring. We test whether this mechanism can reproduce the observed ORC abundance using a Monte Carlo population-synthesis model that combines the galaxy stellar mass function, the radio-AGN incidence relation, dark-matter halo merger histories, and the inflation and buoyant survival of AGN-inflated bubbles, with synthetic radio fluxes and ring geometries drawn from a grid of magnetohydrodynamic SBI simulations. Applying survey-specific selection to the ASKAP-EMU Pilot Survey (944 MHz) and the LOFAR Two-metre Sky Survey (LoTSS; 144 MHz), we predict $2.7^{+3.9}_{-1.6}$ detectable ORCs in the EMU Pilot, matching the three found there, and $268^{+331}_{-148}$ in LoTSS, of which $7.5^{+9.5}_{-4.2}$ have a counterpart at 1.4 GHz. The predicted hosts are mostly central galaxies in group-scale halos. The predicted rings are physically smaller and lie at lower redshifts than the galaxies identified as hosts of the known ORCs, suggesting that SBI produces mainly the nearby part of the ORC population, or that some ORCs are associated with the wrong host. The population synthesis model also predicts a large population of low surface brightness steep-spectrum ORCs in the LoTSS band, implying a large hidden population and predicting that deeper low-frequency surveys should uncover many more ORCs than are currently known. These results indicate that shock-bubble interactions can account for at least part of the observed incidence of ORCs.

title: Modelling kNN-CDFs of biased tracers in redshift space using hybrid Lagrangian bias expansion
summary: Higher-order statistics are becoming increasingly useful in clustering studies of the large-scale structure (LSS) of the universe. The kNN-CDFs are one such higher-order statistic, sensitive to all N-point correlations and easy to compute on data. Utilising their statistical gains for cosmological inference requires modelling them accurately for the tracer of interest. We use the hybrid Lagrangian bias expansion to enable this modelling in redshift space, building and validating the pipeline on Quijote simulations. We show that the kNN-CDFs of a luminous red galaxy (LRG)-like sample can be modelled down to scales as small as r = 10 Mpc/h, with the minimum reliable scale increasing with nearest-neighbour order. Moreover, the model parameters inferred from the kNN-CDFs also describe the galaxy power spectrum P(k), indicating model consistency across the two statistics and the feasibility of combining them. Fisher forecasts for galaxy auto clustering show that combining P(k) and kNN-CDFs improves constraints on all parameters relative to either statistic alone. Relative to P(k), the constraints on $b_3$ improve the most, while those on $σ_8$ and $Ω_m$ improve by factors of 3.5 and 1.7, respectively. Including galaxy-matter cross clustering alongside galaxy auto clustering further improves the Fisher constraints from both P(k) and kNN-CDFs, with their combination yielding the tightest constraints overall. Relative to P(k), the largest improvement from this combination is found for $b_2$, while the constraints on $σ_8$ and $Ω_m$ improve by factors of 4.2 and 1.7, respectively. These results demonstrate the applicability of the hybrid Lagrangian bias framework to model the kNN-CDFs of biased tracers in redshift space, and the potential of combining higher-order and two-point statistics to extract cosmological information.

title: Joint Angular-Power Distributions of Interfering Nanohertz Gravitational Waves
summary: Finite populations of supermassive black-hole binaries produce fluctuations in both gravitational-wave power and pulsar timing correlations. We characterize the realization-dependent, orientation-averaged Earth-term angular correlation through its frequency-resolved Legendre coefficients. A hybrid model of bright sources and a Gaussian faint background extends the conditional Gamma distribution in the many-weak-source limit to non-central $χ^2$ statistics, yielding correlated multipoles after population marginalization. Our analytical variance decomposition and SMBHB population simulations reveal a population-dependent transition from interference dominated variance at low frequencies to population-power-dominated variance at high frequencies. In the many-weak-source regime, a multivariate lognormal approximation captures the main features of the joint distribution using only the first two log-cumulants. These results provide statistical benchmarks for fluctuations in both the overall amplitude and angular structure of the realized correlation.

title: Star clusters at cosmic dawn I: the emergence of the initial cluster mass function
summary: JWST observations of lensed galaxies reveal unusually bright star-cluster candidates within the first billion years after the Big Bang. However, the physical processes shaping the initial cluster mass function (ICMF) remain uncertain. We study the formation of a galaxy embedded in a dark matter halo whose virial mass reaches $10^{10} \mathrm{M}_\odot$ at $z=6$, using cosmological radiation-hydrodynamics zoom-in simulations. Its star clusters, represented by sink particles, accrete gas and form stellar populations that supply radiation and supernova feedback, thereby regulating their own growth. As we do not prescribe an efficiency per free-fall time or a fixed star-cluster formation duration, the ICMF emerges self-consistently. We assess the effects of numerical resolution and stellar radiation. Schechter fits to the central-galaxy ICMF give truncation masses near $6 \times 10^6 \mathrm{M}_\odot$, with substantial uncertainty. At fixed resolution, including stellar radiation makes the low-mass slope of the ICMF shallower, from $-1.60$ to $-1.34$, while doubling the spatial resolution steepens it back to $-1.54$. Stellar radiation also reduces the abundance of low-mass clouds, particularly those with lower gas densities, and shortens the formation time of star clusters to about a Myr, i.e. well before their first supernovae go off. On average, more rapidly fed star clusters accrete for longer, making their final masses rise faster than linearly with the initial accretion rate and contributing to a flatter ICMF. At fixed host-galaxy star formation rate, our brightest simulated clusters reach UV luminosities comparable to those of observed lensed star-cluster candidates.

title: SMMAN Studies of AGN Variability. I. Long-term Spectral Evolution and a Candidate $\sim1000$-day Quasi-periodic Modulation in 4C+72.28
summary: The SMMAN project has carried out nine years of radio flux monitoring in the C and K bands of the blazar 4C+72.28. The two bands show markedly different secular evolution, with a substantially stronger K-band decline producing a gradual decrease in the C-K spectral index. After accounting for this secular evolution, multiple timing diagnostics reveal a candidate quasi-periodic modulation with a characteristic timescale of $\sim1000$ d, most clearly in the C band. The C-band GLSP peak reaches a local significance of $3.29σ$, while its global significance remains modest at $\sim2σ$ and the monitoring baseline covers only about three cycles. Independent and joint MCMC fits support a phenomenological decomposition for both bands into a long-term linear trend and a recurrent component. Under the shared-period assumption, the joint fit returns a characteristic timescale of approximately 1027 d and a similar fractional recurrent amplitudes of $\simeq5.45\%$. Information-criterion comparisons favor the combined linear-plus-sinusoidal model in both bands. Cross-correlation analysis shows a nominal K-leading offset in the original light curves but a centroid consistent with zero lag after detrending, although the lag distributions overlap substantially. These results are consistent with a common recurrent modulation superposed on slower frequency-dependent jet evolution. Geometrical Doppler-factor modulation provides one plausible interpretation, although intrinsic and opacity-related processes cannot be excluded.

title: One-Million-Year-Old Nascent Eclipsing Binaries in the LMC
summary: The light curves of nascent eclipsing binaries (EBs) feature sinusoidal reflection effects as a hot B-type main-sequence (MS) primary irradiates the near side of a cool, low-mass, pre-MS companion. We obtained multi-epoch echelle spectra with the MIKE spectrograph on the 6.5m Magellan-Clay Telescope of three nascent EBs embedded in H II regions within the LMC. By fitting atmospheric models to the spectra, the primaries are found to be mid-B dwarfs (T_eff,1 = 18,600-22,800 K; M_1 = 6.8-8.5 Msun). The dynamical masses of the secondaries are only M_2 = 0.38-0.95 Msun, yielding extremely small mass ratios q = M_2/M_1 = 0.05-0.11. Unlike solar-type primaries, which exhibit a dearth of close companions with q < 0.1 known as the brown dwarf desert, massive stars can readily form with very close companions below q < 0.1. By fitting PHOEBE models to the OGLE-III light curves, we measure the secondary radii R_2 = 2.0-2.8 Rsun and temperatures T_eff,2 = 4,000 K. The pre-MS companions are located high on the Hayashi track where evolutionary models indicate ages of only 1 Myr. Their extreme youth suggests that nascent EBs formed via inward disk migration during the previous embedded protostellar phase.

title: Complete Multi-Band Structural Characterization for 10 Million Galaxies in the Hyper Suprime-Cam Wide Survey using Deep Learning
summary: Galaxy structure is wavelength-dependent, as different photometric bands trace distinct stellar populations and structural components. We present per-galaxy Bayesian posterior distributions of the bulge-to-total light ratio ($L_B/L_T$), effective radius ($R_e$), and flux ($F$) in the $g$, $r$, and $i$ bands for nearly $10$ million galaxies across $\sim$1400\,deg$^2$ of the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program (HSC-SSP) Wide survey at $z \leq 0.75$ and $m < 23$. To our knowledge, this is the largest multi-band catalog of bulge--disk structural parameters with per-galaxy posteriors. $\sim$3.9 million of the above galaxies have full multi-band coverage. Measurements are generated using the Galaxy Morphology Posterior Estimation Network (\gampen{}), a Bayesian deep-learning framework. We demonstrate that we can adapt \gampen{} from previously-trained single-band models to the new bands by using transfer learning on only $\sim$0.5\% of our dataset. Despite this extremely small training set, \gampen{} successfully reproduces light-profile fitting measurements and its output posteriors are extremely well-calibrated with $\lesssim6\%$ mean deviation. This approach offers a scalable pathway to structural parameter measurements with robust uncertainties for Rubin, Euclid, and Roman data, which we will pursue in forthcoming work. While structural measurements remain robust across most bands and redshift ranges, performance degrades significantly for the $g$-band at $z \gtrsim 0.5$, where it increasingly probes rest-frame ultraviolet emission; these measurements are therefore excluded from the public release. This public catalog will enable large-scale statistical studies of morphological color gradients, wavelength-dependent galaxy structure, and galaxy evolution.

title: Research of signs of star formation in three S0 galaxies - members of isolated pairs
summary: We obtained and analyzed long-slit spectra of three lenticular galaxies with optical rings: PGC 48114, ESO 234-011, and ESO 444-076. Ionized gas was detected in all of them. In PGC 48114, the excitation mechanism of the ionized gas differs along the ring, despite the consistent kinematics of the ionized gas and stars, as we showed earlier. Narrow-band images of PGC 48114 in the H$α$ and [NII]$λ$6583 emission lines revealed a star formation arc in the northwestern part of the ring. In ESO 234-011 and ESO 444-076, the ionized gas along the long slit is shock-excited and have kinematic discrepancy with the stars. This implies accretion of matter at an angle to the main disk of the S0 galaxies, which likely inhibits ongoing star formation. The companions of these S0 galaxies are late-type galaxies with extensive ongoing star formation. These companions may be the sources of the gas, or each pair may be feeding from a common gas reservoir.

title: FastSpec: Fast and versatile stellar spectrum synthesis code
summary: Modelling data from modern spectroscopic surveys and time-resolved spectropolarimetric observations requires stellar synthetic spectra to be computed rapidly over wide wavelength ranges from line lists that increasingly reach hundreds of millions of transitions. Spectropolarimetric analyses of magnetically active stars additionally demand a solution of the polarised radiative transfer problem. We present FastSpec, a new LTE spectrum synthesis code designed around two goals: increased raw computational speed and broad astrophysical applicability, including the calculation of the full Stokes vector in the presence of a magnetic field. FastSpec computes emergent intensity and flux spectra from plane-parallel and spherical model atmospheres. Chemical and ionisation equilibrium is obtained from the updated SME equation-of-state package, continuum opacities follow the ATLAS family of routines, hydrogen bound-bound and bound-free absorption uses the occupation-probability formalism, and line absorption is evaluated with fast table-based Voigt and Faraday-Voigt profile algorithms. The transfer equation is integrated with DELO-Bezier formal solvers in both scalar and Stokes-vector form. Speed is achieved through aggressive OpenMP parallelisation, adaptive per-line wavelength windowing, and a memory-capped block-processing scheme that lets arbitrarily large line lists be handled within a user-defined RAM budget. The code synthesises spectra thousands of Å wide from line lists of $10^8$ molecular and atomic transitions in under a minute on a modern multi-core laptop while reproducing benchmark calculations from established codes. FastSpec combines the physical completeness of classical model atmosphere and spectrum synthesis codes with the speed required by large surveys and the polarised transfer needed for stellar magnetism studies into a single portable package.

title: Non-Axisymmetric Pillar Structures due to Embedded Stars in AGN Accretion Discs
summary: Gravitationally unstable outer regions of AGN discs may host in situ formation of massive stars whose heating produces localized vertical "pillars" on the disc surface, in the same region that emits the broad lines. Here we investigate the reverberation-mapping signatures that such pillars would produce. We compute velocity-delay maps $Ψ(λ, τ)$, time-evolving emission-line spectra, and continuum reverberation lag spectra for these structures. We model each pillar as a 2D Gaussian perturbation to the disc height under lamp-post irradiation and weight the line response with Cloudy photoionization grids covering the major BLR lines. We show H$α$, Mg II, and C IV as representative examples. A single pillar produces a localized hotspot in $Ψ$ and a clear "S-wave" pattern in the time-evolving spectrum that persists, though diluted, for $N \sim 100$ pillars. Emission-line fluxes are suppressed in shadows behind the pillars, but when normalized by H$β$ (or by the local continuum) the line-to-H$β$ ratios move in opposite directions: Mg II/H$β$ rises while C IV/H$β$ drops. This contrast distinguishes pillars from purely kinematic features that would modulate all lines by similar factors. Across scans of the pillar shape and lamp-post height, the pillar models produce an optical continuum reverberation lag spectrum of the observed magnitude. The once-per-orbit modulation grows with $\sin i$ from foreshortening, and at sufficiently high inclination the pillar's body geometrically self-occults its lamp-facing inner slope, adding a sharper near/far contrast. These signatures provide observational diagnostics for detecting in situ star formation in AGN discs through velocity-resolved reverberation mapping campaigns.

title: Finite-distance effects and scalar suppression in massive gravity
summary: Pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) probe the stochastic gravitational wave (GW) background through the angular cross-correlations of timing residuals. For a GW background in general relativity (GR), the expected overlap reduction function (ORF) is given by the Hellings--Downs (HD) correlation. We investigate how a nonzero graviton mass modifies this prediction through a massive dispersion relation and additional vector and scalar polarizations, producing a modified effective ORF. In the massive limit, the finite-distance pulsar terms survive angular averaging, multiplying the correlations of all three polarization sectors by a pulsar-dependent factor that can enhance, suppress, or reverse them. We adopt a tensor Earth--Earth normalization that preserves the continuous finite-distance effect. In the massless limit, we find that the vector ORF vanishes and the scalar ORF approaches a finite breathing mode. We propose the phenomenological prescription $Ω_S/Ω_T=A_S(m_g/ω)^{n_S}$, with scalar amplitude parameter $A_S$ and suppression index $n_S>0$. These results provide a consistent framework for future PTA analyses of massive gravity.

title: Galaxy Luminosity Functions at z~7-10 from Four Years of JWST Observations
summary: We present galaxy luminosity functions at $z\approx 7.4$ and 10 based on a comprehensive search for candidate galaxies at $6.4\lesssim z\lesssim11.3$ in JWST's public NIRCam data four years after its operation. Our work utilises nine fields covering $\sim$1,045~arcmin$^2$ in total, including seven blank fields and two galaxy cluster fields. Using the dropout technique, we selected 3,733 dropouts from the F090W passband and 2,396 dropouts from the F115W passband, which constitute the largest samples of candidate galaxies at $z\approx 7.4$ and $z\approx 10$ to date. Among these objects, 338 F090W-dropouts and 99 F115W-dropouts already have secure redshifts from JWST NIRSpec spectroscopy over four years, which we use to form two large spectroscopic subsamples to assess the magnitude-dependent contamination rates of their parent dropout samples. Our luminosity functions are based on the results after statistically correcting for both incompleteness and contamination. We find that the luminosity function at $z\approx 7.4$ can be well described by a conventional Schechter function but with a faint-end slope of $α=-1.70\pm0.16$ that is significantly shallower than most of the previous studies at $z\approx 7$--8. To verify this result, more imaging and spectroscopy at $\sim$30~mag will be needed. The luminosity function at $z\approx 10$, on the other hand, can hardly be fitted by a Schechter function but is more consistent with a power law in the form of $Φ(M)\propto 10^{-0.4(β+1)M}$, with the best-fit slope of $β=-2.36\pm0.16$. While such a behavior is largely driven by the high number densities at $M_{\rm UV}\lesssim -21.8$~mag, it is supported by the currently existing spectroscopic confirmations. Further spectroscopy at the bright end($\lesssim 26$~mag) will be needed to strengthen this result.

title: Polarization Observations of NGC 315 with FAST
summary: We present new continuum and polarization observations of radio galaxy NGC 315 obtained with the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST) over 1.0-1.5 GHz. The FAST data detect diffuse large-scale polarized emission with a noise level of 0.065 mJy beam$^{-1}$ at resolution of $4'$. We derived a rotation measure (RM) map with an error of 1.1 rad m$^{-2}$ including systematic error. The intrinsic RM map was obtained after subtracting the Galactic foreground contribution. We estimated a total magnetic field strength of $\lesssim 1$ $μ$G across the source and a thermal electron density of $\sim 10^{-4}$ cm$^{-3}$ toward the northwest lobe. The fractional polarization analysis suggests a random magnetic-field component over a large area toward the northwest lobe.

title: Forward model of the Gaia DR3 selection function
summary: The completeness of an astronomical catalogue depends on its selection function, which is a combination of the observing strategy, instrumental characteristics, and intrinsic properties of the sources being observed. This is particularly complex for Gaia, whose non-uniform scanning law and onboard prioritisation of bright sources in dense areas make its selection function vary strongly with celestial position and source brightness. We estimate the Gaia DR3 source catalogue selection function across the whole sky and over the full magnitude range, using only data from the Gaia catalogue and knowledge of the nominal scanning law as provided by the Gaia Observation Forecast Tool. We develop a hierarchical Bayesian model that estimates the number of times Gaia scanned each celestial position jointly with the source detection efficiency, and fit it via Markov chain Monte Carlo to the 1 806 196 447 sources in Gaia DR3 with reported celestial positions, G magnitudes, and astrometric matched transit counts. Gaia DR3 is essentially complete for G in (5, 19.5) in the on-sky median. After that, the completeness decreases with magnitude according to the scanning law pattern combined with the imprint of crowded regions. The completeness is also lower at the very bright end of the survey, consistent with the known limitations on Gaia observations of bright stars. We find an unexpected completeness increase beyond G ~ 21, which we conclude is an artefact caused by extended sources, as confirmed by cross-matching against Euclid's Q1 catalogue. Treating the scanning law as part of the inference process, and anchoring it to all Gaia DR3 sources of all magnitudes on a fine-grained grid on the sky, removes the need for an explicit crowding correction. The resulting selection function, valid everywhere where Gaia data are available, is released as part of the GaiaUnlimited Python package. [abridged]

title: Local Analogs of Little Red Dots: Clues to the X-ray Weakness
summary: A major question about JWST's little red dots (LRDs) at $z\sim4-8$ is the origin of their apparent X-ray weakness. Even deep Chandra stacks yield only tentative detections or broad-band limits and cannot distinguish among super-Eddington accretion, intrinsic X-ray weakness, and Compton-thick (CT) obscuration. Local analogs offer a powerful complementary route. At $z\sim0.3$, similarly luminous sources require $\sim10^{3-4}$ less exposure for comparable signal-to-noise, suffer less source confusion, and directly probe the diagnostic rest-frame soft X-rays. Here we present a pilot Einstein Probe/FXT study of six "local little red dots" (LLRDs), V-shaped broad-line green pea galaxies selected as low-redshift counterparts of LRDs. These sources show X-ray diversity: "X-normal" LLRDs resemble type 1 AGNs in X-ray luminosity and optical variability, whereas the "X-weak" stack lies $\sim0.5-0.7$ dex below standard unobscured-quasar scaling relations while remaining compatible with the representative LRD stack and 95% of published individual limits. The X-weak LLRDs also lack detected optical variability and have redder optical continua than X-normal LLRDs, making their V-shaped SEDs closer to those of high-redshift LRDs. The detection of the X-weak stack at $\sim3.3σ$ with the soft-X-ray-sensitive EP-FXT provides rest-frame $\sim2-3$ keV constraints difficult to reconcile with a typical unobscured super-Eddington model or a local-AGN-like CT geometry examined here, although modified variants remain possible. The simplest alternative is a mildly X-ray-weak corona ($Δα_{\mathrm{ox}}\sim-0.1$ to $-0.2$) with Compton-thin absorption ($N_{\mathrm{H}}\sim10^{22-23}$ cm$^{-2}$), consistent with the independent Balmer decrement/break diagnostics. Together with growing samples of local LRD analogs, our results offer a practical path for testing the physical nature of LRD X-ray weakness.

title: Introducing the GION Lightcone Simulation Suite for Multi-Wavelength Large-Scale Structure Cosmology
summary: We present the GION (Ginkaku Lightcone Multi-wavelength Simulation Project) simulation suite: 10 full-sky high-resolution cosmological lightcone simulations and their associated products for multi-wavelength large-scale structure cosmology. We use the TreePM $N$-body code GINKAKU, which is highly optimized in the massively parallel environment, and integrate the on-the-fly lightcone construction technique. Each lightcone simulation is run with $6144^3$ particles in a volume of $(1.5 \, h^{-1} \, \mathrm{Gpc})^3$, which corresponds to a particle mass of $1.28 \times 10^9 \, h^{-1} \, \mathrm{M}_\odot$, and extends to $z = 5$. The fine mass resolution and the depth of the lightcone simulations allow us to resolve dark matter halos down to $10^{11} \, h^{-1} \, \mathrm{M}_\odot$ in the high-redshift Universe, which is crucial for applications to the Stage-IV cosmological surveys. The fundamental statistics of the simulations, including the matter power spectrum, halo power spectrum, and halo mass function, are validated against theoretical predictions. We also generate various large-scale structure observables from the lightcone outputs: the dark matter halo catalogs, mock galaxy samples, weak lensing convergence maps, and thermal and kinematic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (tSZ and kSZ) maps. The angular power spectra of these observables, including the cross-correlation between weak lensing and the tSZ effect, are in good agreement with theoretical predictions, demonstrating that the suite provides mutually consistent multi-wavelength observables on the same lightcone. The GION simulation suite will be publicly available and can be used for various cosmological analyses to address the observational systematic effects and validate theoretical models.

title: The Galactic Center Reference Frame: A 30-Year Solution
summary: Stellar orbits probe the metric of and mass around the Sgr A* massive black hole. To enable study of the black hole, the surrounding mass, and tests of gravity, a precise reference frame must be established and maintained. We present an updated stellar maser-based reference frame for the inner parsec of the Galactic Center, referenced to the radio continuum of Sgr A*. This work synthesizes 30 years of astrometric observations of 15 SiO stellar masers and the Sgr A* continuum at 43 GHz. The uncertainty in the mean offset of the maser ensemble from Sgr A* is 0.08 mas in the current epoch and will decay to 0.10 mas by 2030. At a distance of 8.2 kpc, these correspond to position uncertainties of 0.6 AU and 0.8 AU, respectively, which is similar to or smaller than the stellar SiO-emitting region. The mean maser proper motion uncertainties are 0.05 mas yr$^{-1}$ in RA and 0.08 mas yr$^{-1}$ in Dec, corresponding to 1.8 km s$^{-1}$ and 3.2 km s$^{-1}$. The reference frame stability between IR and maser astrometry is 10~$μ$as yr$^{-1}$ (0.40 km s$^{-1}$) in RA and 15 $μ$as yr$^{-1}$ (0.57 km s$^{-1}$) in Dec. The masers show substantial variability in flux density and velocity structure, most notably IRS~7, which shows a 30-fold brightening in a blueshifted component since 2022. This variability may set a floor on future astrometry improvements and especially measurements of radial acceleration.

title: Alignment-driven binary evolution in warped circumbinary discs: 3D moving-mesh hydrodynamics of eccentric and inclined binaries
summary: We present three-dimensional moving-mesh hydrodynamical simulations (\arepo{}) of equal-mass binaries in circumbinary discs, spanning binary eccentricity ($e = 0.0,\,0.3,\,0.6$) and inclination ($i = 0^\circ$--$60^\circ$), using a locally isothermal $α$-disc ($H/r = α_{\rm visc} = 0.1$) with fixed Keplerian orbits. Discs above the critical inclination $i_{\rm crit}(e)$, decreasing with $e$, drive their interiors near-polar, so eccentricity alone alters the outcome at fixed $i$. Discs reach polar alignment ten times faster than they align toward the binary plane, settling long before the binary's orbit responds. Alignment dictates how the disc acts on the binary. First, a disc tilting back toward the binary plane spends nearly all its torque reorienting the binary's orbit, whereas a disc driven polar redirects it into the orbit itself, which shrinks 10--20 times faster. Second, at $e = 0.6$ the turn to polar is a single transient reshaping the accretion flow, cavity and orbit, with accretion enhanced ($i = 45^\circ$) or suppressed ($i = 60^\circ$). Third, misalignment suppresses coplanar eccentricity pumping: the attractor at $e \approx 0.4$ survives only below $i \approx 15^\circ$, so misaligned binaries circularise and may enter the gravitational-wave regime less eccentric than coplanar models predict. Around a circular binary, the familiar $\approx 4.5$-orbit accretion modulation vanishes while the disc is strongly warped, returning as it realigns, a time-domain signature of misaligned massive black-hole binaries. Finally, observed polar discs around stellar binaries, such as HD~98800~BaBb's, are likely in their final state; intermediate misalignments reflect slower alignment toward the binary plane.

title: An Extra-nuclear Water Maser in NGC 1106 Likely Driven By An AGN Shock: Implications for Maser-based Black Hole Mass Measurements
summary: We present Very Large Array A-configuration ($0.13$'') 22 GHz spectral-line and continuum observations of the Swift-BAT detected Seyfert 2 galaxy, NGC 1106, aimed at localizing a water maser line offset from the host systemic velocity by 541 km s$^{-1}$. The 22 GHz continuum emission reveals a 352 pc extended structure within the nucleus of NGC 1106, and we spatially resolve the water maser emission to a compact region $\sim1$ kpc ($3.12$'') from the nucleus. Comparing our data with previous 22 GHz 1'' observations, we found that the water maser lies near the boundary of a radio extension aligned with the jet axis, likely arising from the interface between the active galactic nucleus (AGN) outflow and the host galaxy's ISM. To verify this, we compared the water maser in NGC 1106 to a known water maser in a star-forming region within the Milky Way, along with known extragalactic water masers associated with star formation and AGN driven outflows. Overall, we found that the maser position, velocity offset, flux density, and alignment with the jet axis are consistent with an origin at the interface between the AGN outflow and the host ISM. Our results have important implications for maser-based black hole mass measurements in which disk geometry is ambiguous. Since single-dish observations cannot spatially separate disk masers from outflow-driven masers, high-velocity maser features attributed to the accretion disk may also include contributions from kpc-scale shocks.

title: Spatial distribution of star formation in dwarf galaxies: Merger-driven and secular starburst
summary: Galaxy interactions can induce bursts of star formation (SF), while internal or secular processes can also trigger starbursts (SB). Recent studies of the spatial distribution of SF in high-mass (M$_{*}>10^{10}M_{\odot}$) SB galaxies show that SF is centrally concentrated in merger-driven SBs, whereas in secularly driven SB systems, SF is uniformly enhanced across the system. However, it is not clear whether such distinct spatial signatures are present in low-mass (M$_{*} < 10^{10} M_{\odot}$) SB galaxies. In this context, we studied the SF properties of a sample of 272 isolated SB (i.e., with no massive galaxy, within a 1 Mpc$^3$ volume) dwarf galaxies consisting of 17 post-merger and 255 non-interacting SB galaxies, spanning a stellar mass range of $10^{7}-10^{9.6} M_{\odot}$ and a redshift range of 0.01-0.12. For this study, we utilise FUV imaging data from GALEX to estimate the star formation rates of our sample galaxies. We investigated the spatial variation of SB activity by comparing star formation rate surface density (SFRD) across radial bins for post-merger and non-interacting samples of dwarfs. We find an enhancement in SFRD across all radial bins for both samples, and that the enhancement is more or less uniform across the galaxy, within uncertainties. This indicates that SF in low-mass SB galaxies is uniformly enhanced throughout the galaxy, regardless of the mechanism that triggers the SB. This contrasts with observations in massive galaxies, where SF is centrally concentrated in merger-driven SB systems. The lack of central concentration of SF in low-mass merger systems could be due to their shallow gravitational potentials and the compression of extended gaseous envelopes during interactions, which trigger SF across these galaxies. Deeper, higher-spatial-resolution observations are essential for better understanding the spatial distribution of SF in low-mass galaxies.

title: Gauge-field energy density in inflationary kinetic-coupling models: QFT regularization versus horizon cutoffs
summary: Coupling gauge fields to the inflaton can amplify their quantum fluctuations during inflation, with potential applications to a range of cosmological phenomena. A central challenge is to define finite and physically meaningful observables, such as the gauge-field energy density. In this work, we study an Abelian gauge field kinetically coupled to the inflaton through $f^2(φ)F_{μν}F^{μν}$ in a de Sitter background with $f\propto a^{γ_1}$, and compare conventional quantum-field-theoretic regularization with horizon-cutoff prescriptions. Using a hard physical-momentum cutoff and dimensional regularization, we derive the ultraviolet divergences in closed form and fix the remaining one-parameter finite-part ambiguity by requiring the coupling-induced total energy density to be nonnegative. We then examine five horizon-cutoff prescriptions based on characteristic scales of the mode equations. Their predictions depend sensitively on the choice of horizon scale and, for weak gauge-field production, can deviate substantially from the regularized result; for the adopted finite-part prescription, the minimal horizon agrees best with the regularized total energy density. As $|γ_1|\to 2$, where infrared modes dominate, the relative deviation of all prescriptions from the regularized result vanishes, independently of the finite-part prescription. Outside this regime, the separate electric and magnetic contributions, which can become negative after regularization, are not reliably reproduced by any of the horizon-cutoff prescriptions.

title: The MIRI/MRS Library. III. Detector-based optimal spectral extraction and high-contrast imaging applications
summary: (Abridged) JWST has now been operational for five years, and the associated data reduction pipelines have reached maturity. For MIRI/MRS, one can generally get a good-quality spectrum by simply running the standard pipeline, especially for unresolved sources. However, users are starting to look deeper into the data, trying to detect the smallest features in the faintest objects, and find close companions. Following the corrections derived in Papers I and II in this series, we now introduce a novel way to extract MIRI/MRS spectra: from the detectors directly. Currently the most common way to analyse data from integral field spectrometers is to reconstruct a spectral cube from the detector images. Theoretically, detector-extracted spectra could reach higher S/N, and better handle bad pixels. We generate stable and well-sampled PSF models using the sub-pixel scan of calibration star 10 Lac observed in PID 3779. These PSFs were used in a detector-based optimal extraction algorithm building on past approaches, where the contributions per pixel were weighted by their noise properties and contribution to the total illumination. The PSF models were used to subtract the PSF of a bright central source from the detector, both by direct subtraction, and a PCA approach. We find that our optimal setup allows us to get a $>$1.5 times higher S/N compared to the standard pipeline cube extraction. However, we approximately matched more involved cube processing. We were able to subtract the PSF to sub-percent levels, allowing us to extract spectra from faint companions. The novel approach greatly improves on the current standard pipeline reduction. We have not yet reached the fundamental noise limits. There are clear points of improvement that can be addressed using additional data. We demonstrate that detector-based processing of MIRI/MRS data has great potential.

title: Magnetic Reconnection Modifies Cosmic-Ray Transport in the Interstellar Medium
summary: We present numerical magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations of the interstellar medium in gravity-stratified boxes with the Piernik MHD code. The system contains thermal gas, spectrally resolved cosmic-ray (CR) nuclei within the CRESP algorithm, and spectrally unresolved CR protons. CR protons drive gas outflows and undergo Coulomb and hadronic losses. CR nuclei undergo Coulomb losses. We also include the spallation of primary Carbon by thermal gas atoms, thereby decaying Car- bon into secondary stable Boron isotopes. We use the resistive-MHD approximation as a subgrid model for unresolved turbulent magnetic dissipation in current sheets. We perform a parameter study of the magnetic diffusivity η. The Boron-to-Carbon ratio B/C and hadronic γ-ray luminosity density are computed as diagnostics. We find that non-zero magnetic diffusivity modifies the magnetic topology, leading to a more horizontal field in the halo, thereby accumulating CRs in the disk region and signifi- cantly increasing the CR escape time. As a consequence, the local turbulent conditions and turbulent reconnection in the interstellar medium should be considered when interpreting B/C and hadronic γ-ray luminosity observed at Earth. Our results suggest that the escape time and diffusion coefficient of CRs deduced from observational data in the vicinity of the Solar System cannot be extrapolated to the whole Galaxy.

title: ExoVetter and a TESS Exoplanet Transit Search of Kepler Stars as Ground Truth
summary: We introduce a Python package called exoVetter that produces vetting metrics and visualizations to evaluate transiting exoplanet signals found in high-cadence time-series photometry. exoVetter is open source, modular, and independent of the mission data so that it can be easily expanded and used as part of different transit search pipelines tuned to different science cases and missions. We demonstrate its use in a pipeline as a way to distinguish real events found in a box-least squares exoplanet transit search of 324,530 light curves from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite mission; we limit our demonstration to stars also observed by the more sensitive Kepler telescope as a way to establish ground truth for the events found in the light curves. Using this ground truth, we provide baseline thresholds for several flux-level vetters and one centroid-offset vetter when using exoVetter metrics on TESS data. Our demonstration also indicates that it is possible to create a planet catalog from the light curves of dim targets (>13.5Tmag) that has a similar fraction of real events to that of the bright targets (<13.5Tmag) for short period events identified in the TESS-Gaia light curves.

title: The Galactic Center Gamma-Ray Excess and the Look-Elsewhere Effect
summary: The origin of the excess of GeV gamma-rays in the Milky Way's galactic center observed by Fermi-LAT has been an open question for nearly two decades. The two leading interpretations of this signal are that it is produced either by annihilating dark matter (DM), or arises from unresolved point sources, such as a novel population of millisecond pulsars. In both scenarios, uncertainties and limitations in the modeling of galactic diffuse gamma-ray emission, such as the steady-state approximation of cosmic ray (CR) propagation and assumption of an axisymmetric distribution of CRs, complicate the interpretation of the galactic center excess (GCE). Simulations with full magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) and CR transport can provide a new avenue for understanding the astrophysical phenomena that drive galactic diffuse gamma-ray emission. We utilize MHD simulations of Milky Way analogs with time-dependent, spectrally-resolved CR transport to reconstruct diffuse gamma-ray emission. Comparing instantaneous emission to a time-averaged baseline, we find residuals up to several times larger than the Fermi GCE, with a wide range of spectral shapes and spatial morphologies. At some simulation snapshots, the spectrum and morphology of the residuals resemble the Fermi GCE. Our results suggest that the Fermi GCE may be a manifestation of the look-elsewhere effect- a transient fluctuation in diffuse emission from stellar sources, observed at an inopportune moment- and motivate the development of new Fermi-LAT analysis templates that account for time-dependent CR transport.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks vs U-Net: Application to thermal dust emission recovery in the microwave
summary: Galactic thermal dust emission is the dominant foreground contaminant of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) at frequencies above 100 GHz, and its accurate separation is essential for current and future CMB experiments. Deep learning methods, in particular convolutional architectures such as the U-Net, have demonstrated strong performance for CMB component separation, but typically operate as purely data-driven models with no explicit enforcement of the physical laws governing the emission they reconstruct. In this work, we present a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) that embeds the Modified Black Body (MBB) spectral model as a hard, differentiable architectural constraint, and we compare it against a standard U-Net baseline trained under an identical pipeline. Both architectures are trained on realistic simulated Planck HFI patches at four frequencies (143, 217, 353 and 545 GHz) and evaluated on a shared validation set as well as on three independent Galactic dust realizations from the PySM phenomenological dust models named D4, D7 and D10. We find that both networks achieve comparable reconstruction quality across all evaluated datasets, with a Structural Similarity Index Measure consistently above 0.96 and a fitted angular power-spectrum spectral index that agrees with the input to within 1% in every region. Embedding the physical constraint in the PINN does not measurably degrade reconstruction accuracy relative to the unconstrained U-Net, while additionally guaranteeing that every predicted output corresponds to a thermodynamically admissible physical configuration. These results establish the physics-informed formulation as a viable methodological alternative for dust component separation, providing physical interpretability without a trade-off in reconstruction fidelity.

title: A probabilistic approach to separate mergers and jellyfish galaxies: Application of morphological non-parametric indexes to the DESI Legacy Survey
summary: Galaxy morphology traces the physical processes that shape galaxy evolution, but non-parametric diagnostic boundaries depend on image quality and preprocessing. We investigate the classification of regular spirals, regular ellipticals, mergers, and jellyfish (ram-pressure-stripping candidate) galaxies in the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys. Using galmex measurements of ten non-parametric morphological indices, we evaluate two-dimensional diagnostic planes with a cross-validated Bayesian kernel-density classifier and combine all indices using probability-calibrated LightGBM models. For separating regular spirals, regular ellipticals, and perturbed systems, the most informative planes combine Shannon entropy with $M_{20}$ or asymmetry indices, reaching balanced accuracies of 0.76-0.77. We provide survey-specific probabilistic boundaries in the entropy-$M_{20}$ and entropy-shape-asymmetry planes. Separating mergers from jellyfish candidates is more challenging; the best two-dimensional combinations, all involving concentration, reach balanced accuracies of approximately 0.73. The calibrated three-class LightGBM model achieves a balanced accuracy and macro-F1 score of 0.89, while the four-class model achieves 0.75 and 0.76, respectively. We provide class probabilities and preferred classifications for 1,744,454 galaxies. Our results show that non-parametric morphology identifies broad structural disturbance reliably, but distinguishing its physical origin is harder: jellyfish candidates occupy a relatively coherent region of parameter space, whereas mergers span diverse and overlapping morphologies.

title: The Physics of the Cold and Warm Interstellar Medium Through Radio Recombination Lines
summary: The interplay between star formation and the interstellar medium (ISM) gives rise to a feedback cycle that is one of the key drivers of galaxy evolution. The coldest gas in the ISM provides the fuel for star formation, and, in turn, the ISM is affected by feedback in the form of photons, shocks, and cosmic rays. Radio recombination lines (RRLs) offer a unique way of characterizing the gas in the ISM as extinction free probes of the gas kinematics, density, temperature, and radiation field. Hydrogen RRLs (HRRLs) probe gas where hydrogen is ionized, while carbon RRLs (CRRLs) probe cold gas in the HI-to-H$_{2}$ transition layers. The superb sensitivity, spatial resolution, large field of view, and frequency resolution and coverage of the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) will allow for efficient observations of RRLs, that will make significant impacts to the study of the diffuse ISM. By observing RRLs with the SKA we will be able to determine the thermal and turbulent balance, chemical enrichment, sizes, and ionization rate of the cold and ionized gases from degree-scales down to arcsecond scales in our Galaxy.

title: ARENA: Active Region attENtion Aggregation for interpretable solar flare prediction
summary: Predicting solar flares is a challenging space-weather forecasting problem with potentially significant impacts on Earth's upper atmosphere, including disruptions to radio communications. We propose Active Region attENtion Aggregation (ARENA), a neural network architecture that predicts solar flares from a variable number of active-region cutouts while learning to identify the region most relevant to the prediction. ARENA is trained using multiple-instance learning under weak supervision, requiring only a flare/no-flare label for the observation and no labels specifying the flare origin. The learned attention mechanism therefore provides a means of localizing the active region driving the prediction without explicit origin annotations. ARENA achieves a heidke skill score of 0.45 which is comparable to other flare prediction approaches. These results demonstrate that active-region-based aggregation can provide an efficient and interpretable approach to solar flare prediction. The code is available at https://github.com/LuisBauer22/ARENA.

title: Systematic Slopes in NIRSpec BOTS Observations
summary: We investigate empirical white light and spectroscopic trends in the temporal systematic slopes seen in NIRSpec Bright Object Time Series (BOTS) observations. Using a sample of 14 high-resolution G395H (dispersed across both the NRS1 and NRS2 detectors) and 10 low-resolution Prism (dispersed across NRS1 only) transit light curves, we measured the visit-long, pre-transit, and post-transit slopes. For the G395H white light curves, we find a correlation between the G395H NRS1 systematic slope and the host star magnitude, as well as the number of groups per integration. We also note that the systematic slopes vary with time over the course of a given time-series, with steeper pre-transit slopes compared to post-transit. These trends in the white light slopes are not apparent for G395H NRS2 or Prism. At the spectroscopic light curve level, the NRS1 and Prism slopes show a distinct wavelength-dependent signature across the full sample with the largest slopes between ~3-3.4 microns. At these wavelengths, the brightest targets display the strongest chromatic slope signatures. The NRS2 slopes show no apparent chromaticity across the full sample.

title: Stochastic dynamics of cosmological inflation in general relativity
summary: The theory of Inflation, supplemented by fluctuations of the quantum vacuum, is the leading paradigm to explain the correlations of inhomogeneities at very large distances in the Universe. Particle physics methods fail when strong non-linearity and non-perturbativity are involved, leaving a whole landscape of untestable scenarios of inflation. Starobinsky's stochastic inflation can in principle treat inflationary inhomogeneities nonlinearly and classically as the Hubble radius becomes smaller than their wavelengths, but it was never formulated in full general relativity, which motivates this thesis. Using the Keldysh formalism of nonequilibrium quantum field theory, we first develop a validity criterion for the use of classical computations, and thus simulations, to probe inflationary interactions, finding analytically that the bispectrum can be extracted from slightly sub-Hubble scales in quasi-de Sitter spacetimes. We then provide the first analytical solutions to the constraints for inhomogeneous initial conditions of numerical relativity simulations of inflation, and use them to explore its nonperturbative regime. Our main contribution is to obtain stochastic equations for the full set of inflaton equations in general relativity: this description incorporates the full nonlinear and backreacting evolution, is small-gauge-invariant, and is free of historical assumptions such as the gradient-free separate universe approximation. We implement these equations in the BSSN formulation of numerical relativity, demonstrating their correctness in slow-roll and ultra slow-roll scenarios via the satisfaction of the constraints, with a first look at eternal inflation. Finally, we extend our coarse-graining methods beyond General Relativity and single-field inflation, offering a phenomenological framework with the ambition of serving as a numerical particle collider for the early universe.

title: The Galactic rotation curve from the ALS III catalogue of OB Stars
summary: The Galactic rotation curve reveals the radial mass distribution of the Milky Way, but its determination depends on the tracer population. Young massive stars are the least dynamically evolved tracer, retaining the kinematics of the gas from which they formed, yet previous determinations from OB stars were confined to the solar neighbourhood. We determine the rotation curve and the solar motion from 14017 spectroscopically confirmed OB stars from the ALS III catalogue, using Gaia DR3 five-dimensional astrometry with revised distances and corrected proper motions. The curve is parameterised as a fourth-degree Chebyshev polynomial in Galactocentric radius and fitted to the proper motions by weighted least squares, solving simultaneously for the solar motion. Uncertainties are derived from 1000 bootstrap resamplings. We obtain a circular velocity at the solar radius (8.178 kpc) of 236.3 +/- 1.1 km/s, solar motion components U = 8.06 +/- 0.41, V = 10.91 +/- 0.86 and W = 7.53 +/- 0.14 km/s, and Oort constants A = 16.35 +/- 0.21 and B = -12.54 +/- 0.19 km/s/kpc. The curve rises inside the solar circle and declines gently beyond it, with a local gradient of -3.81 +/- 0.38 km/s/kpc, and is constrained between 5.5 and 11 kpc. Because the tracer is dynamically cold and the proper motions are fitted directly, no asymmetric drift correction or Jeans modelling is required, so the systematics differ from those affecting older tracers. The gentle decline beyond the solar radius agrees with determinations from older tracers where they overlap, making it unlikely to be a methodological artefact. Only the solar radial motion is poorly constrained by tangential data, without affecting the curve. The stars departing most from the curve (1474 to 1662, depending on the selection criterion) form the largest sample of OB runaway candidates to date, to be analysed in a forthcoming paper based on Gaia DR4.

title: Luminosity-weighted galaxy and gravitational wave cross-correlations
summary: Cross-correlations of galaxies and gravitational waves (GW) can be used to extract cosmological parameters and the gravitational wave bias. In this work, we study how to include galaxy luminosities in these spatial cross-correlations, inspired by the standard approach of dark sirens line-of-sight redshift priors. We present a formalism to include luminosity information in galaxy-GW simulations and study the effects of assigning a hosting probability that depends on luminosity through a simple power law $p_{\rm{host}} \propto L^β$ with $β\in \{0,1,2\}$ corresponding to uniformly, linear and quadratically weighted in luminosity. This effectively changes the GW linear bias with respect to dark matter and, in principle, allows to gain signal-to-noise and a sharper measurement of cosmological parameters. For a realistic luminosity dependence of the galaxy bias taken from DESI data, the gain is marginal, making the method robust to different luminosity weighting prescriptions. We show that the cross-correlation inference is able to recover the injected GW bias within $10\%$ if there is a mismatch between the injected linear bias of host galaxies and observed galaxies, provided that one sticks to relatively large scales. We also show that the Hubble constant and matter energy density can be recovered to $0.5\%$ and $5\%$ respectively with a third generation network of GW detectors, regardless of the modeling of the GW bias.

title: Differential and integral scaling laws of the mass density of molecular clouds
summary: In this work we investigate the mass density - size scaling law in molecular clouds (MCs). This relation reflects the fractal nature of MCs and plays a key role for understanding the physics, structure and evolution of these objects. We make use of the notion "ensemble of MCs", introduced in our previous work (Donkov, Veltchev \& Klessen, 2017), in which all MCs with the same probability density function (PDF) of mass density and effective size are represented by an abstract spherical cloud with the same PDF and size. In this spirit, the model is built on the base of abstract scales of the clouds' substructures (which are simply the radii of the spherical object). We consider two forms of the mass density - size scaling law: differential and integral, which in turn reveal the local and the global fractal clouds' structure. Both scaling functions are characterized by their scaling exponents, which can be explicitly expressed by the PDF of mass density, in the general case. Moreover, we derive a first order linear differential equation connecting the two scaling exponents and obtain its exact solution. As examples we apply this abstract construction to two PDFs: the so called power-law tail and the log-normal. Both have great importance for MC structure and evolution, as the latter corresponds to the earlier stages of clouds' evolution, when supersonic turbulence dominates the physical processes, while the former describes the latest stages of evolution, when star-formation takes place. The obtained results for the scaling exponents in both examples are qualitatively and numerically consistent with respective observations and simulations of MCs.

title: The Impact of Inclination, Redshift, and Mass Ratio Selection on Cosmological Constraints from Bright Sirens Beyond Conventional Fisher Approximations
summary: Future generations of gravitational-wave observatories are projected to detect up to thousands bright siren events within a decade of operation. However, the precision of these cosmological forecasts depends heavily on the astrophysical assumptions embedded within the simulation pipelines. In this work, we systematically investigate the impact of variations in the binary mass ratio ($q$), the maximum observable inclination angle ($ι_{\max}$), and the maximum redshift ($z_{\max}$) on the constraints of the Hubble constant ($H_0$) and the matter density parameter ($Ω_m$). We perform our analyses based on the GWDALI framework, the GW Doublet Approximation, and the phenomenological waveform approximant IMRPhenomD. By adopting sets of non-spinning binary neutron star populations we explore the impact of astrophysical parameters on the constraints of cosmological parameters. Our results reveal a clear dichotomy in the observational requirements: while the statistical uncertainty on $H_0$ falls below the falls below approximately $1.3\%$ level for $N \ge 400$ events and drops under $0.9\%$ once $N \ge 800$, a deep-redshift catalog ($z_{\max} \ge 1.0$) is strictly required to effectively break parameter degeneracies and constrain the global geometry through $Ω_m$. Furthermore, expanding the maximum inclination cutoff from the conservative $20^{\circ}$ up to $40^{\circ}$ substantially mitigates the correlation between distance and inclination.

title: AMICO galaxy clusters in KiDS-1000: Cosmological constraints from the two-point correlation function
summary: In this paper we study the clustering properties of an optically identified photometric galaxy cluster catalogue from KiDS-1000. The sample was identified by the AMICO algorithm and consists of 9049 clusters with $S/N\geq3.5$, in the redshift range $0.1\leq z<0.8$, spread over an effective area of 838.78 deg$^2$. Clusters are selected according to their observed intrinsic richness, with thresholds of $λ^*{obs}\geq 20,25,30$ within $0.10\leq z<0.30$, $0.30\leq z<0.45$ and $0.45\leq z<0.80$, respectively. We measure the multipoles of the two-point correlation function over different ranges of scales from 5 $h^{-1}$ Mpc to 150 $h^{-1}$ Mpc. We model the clustering signal in the context of the $Λ$CDM cosmology, accounting for the main observational effects, such RSDs and photo-$z$ uncertainties. The effective bias of the cluster sample is estimated via a mass-richness scaling relation. For the MCMC analysis, we adopt Gaussian priors on the parameters of the mass-richness scaling relation, and broad, uniform priors to derive cosmological constraints on the cold matter density parameter, the power spectrum amplitude and the structure growth parameter, $S_8\equivσ_8 \sqrt{Ω{m}/0.3}$. Specifically, we find $Ω_{m}=0.24^{+0.02}{-0.02}$ and $σ_8=0.86^{+0.13}{-0.10}$ representing an improvement in precision over both the 2D and 3D AMICO clustering analyses performed on the previous KiDS data release. Moreover, we obtain $S_8=0.77^{+0.10}_{-0.08}$ in $1σ$ agreement with the AMICO KiDS-1000 number counts constraints estimated from the same catalogue, as well as with some results from external early- and late-Universe data sets. Our work strengthens the potential of cluster clustering as a complementary and competitive probe, to be included and further developed with the final KiDS-Legacy data release, and in other future Stage-IV photometric redshift surveys.

title: Collapsars Are Not Heavy $r$-Process Factories
summary: Collapsar disks are proposed sources of $r$-process elements, but neutron-rich disk ejecta require gas to be both neutronized in the disk and ejected before accretion. The magnetic field that enables ejection also thickens the disk and accelerates the inflow, lowering both the density and the time available for weak processing. To compute the resulting neutronization, we evolve the electron fraction of the inflowing gas, adopting at each radius the temperature that maximizes the net neutronization rate for the local density and instantaneous composition. This yields a lower limit on $Y_{\rm e}$ that is independent of the disk's thermal history. We adopt an optimistic unbinding radius of $R_{\rm unb}=10\,r_g$ for all magnetic fluxes capable of launching outflows. Combining this ejection condition with favorable assumptions of low black hole mass, ejection of midplane gas, and the upper end of the $γ$-ray burst (GRB) engine-power scale, which limits the accretion rate to $\dot M_{\rm BH}\lesssim0.4\,M_\odot\,{\rm s}^{-1}$, gives a fiducial lower bound $Y_{\rm e}\gtrsim0.33$, above the characteristic $Y_{\rm e}\approx 0.25$ threshold for heavy $r$-process production. Stronger magnetic flux, toward which jet-launching engines evolve, raises the lower bound to $Y_{\rm e}\gtrsim0.49$. We conclude that collapsar disk outflows cannot supply the heavy $r$-process yields invoked for a dominant enrichment channel. Only engines with unusually high accretion rates, potentially including exceptionally luminous GRBs, such as GRB 221009A, and direct-horizon collapsars, may produce heavy $r$-process ejecta.

title: A Study of the 30 May 2026 Meteor Event Employing Data from Raspberry Boom Infrasound Sensors in the Boston Area
summary: Infrasound signals of one and a half cycles of a 0.4 Hz pressure pulse were detected from the 30 May 2026 meteor over Cape Cod Bay at several university and private Raspberry Boom sensors in the Greater Boston area. Our analyses of these signals demonstrate the ability to define directivity to the source of the event based on differences in the timing of the signals, to determine its identity and location by analysis of the relationship between event distance and sensor event timing, and event acoustical power by the infrasonic pressures measured at the sensor sites. The infrasound event is determined to be the atmospheric fireball blast at between 40 and 50 km in altitude with acoustic energy on the order of 5% to 14% of the total fireball energy.

title: Non-Markovian Cosmology with Causal Memory Kernels
summary: We investigate a non-Markovian extension of Friedmann cosmology in which the present expansion rate retains information about the past cosmic evolution through a causal memory kernel, with \LCDM{} recovered in the limit of vanishing kernel amplitude, $A\to0$. We show that five kernels (Linear, Power Law, Exponential, Gaussian and Oscillatory) arise as cosine transforms of the spectral densities of an unresolved hidden sector, and that the Exponential and Linear kernels also follow independently from Israel-Stewart causal viscosity and from Deser-Woodard non-local gravity, respectively. We constrain the kernels with 30 Cosmic Chronometer (CC) measurements and with $H(z)$ derived from the DESI DR1 and DR2 baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) data, using multi-start $χ^{2}$ minimisation followed by Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling, and compare them with \LCDM{} through the Akaike and Bayesian information criteria. The Linear amplitude is consistent with zero ($A=0.002\pm0.030$ for CC+DR2). The Power-law, Exponential and Gaussian kernels are observationally degenerate: the data select sharply peaked kernels that constrain only an integrated amplitude $\Aeff\simeq0.01$--$0.03$, equivalent to a uniform $0.5$--$1.5\%$ rescaling of $H(z)$, and they are disfavoured relative to \LCDM{} ($Δ{\rm AIC}=+2.5$ to $+3.6$). Only the Oscillatory kernel improves the fit appreciably ($\dchi=4.5$--$8.1$), but it requires a negative damping rate, which is incompatible with the causal derivations, and it is not favoured once CC data are included ($Δ{\rm BIC}=+4.4$ to $+6.2$)

title: Semi-Analytic Predictions for Strong-Lensing Perturbers in Cold and Self-Interacting Dark Matter
summary: Strong gravitational lensing is sensitive to the abundance and internal structure of dark matter halos, providing a probe of gravothermal evolution in self-interacting dark matter (SIDM). We combine semi-analytic cold dark matter (CDM) subhalo histories with a model for gravothermal evolution in SIDM to generate CDM and SIDM subhalo populations across SIDM parameter space. We predict their projected enclosed masses and deflection-based projected density slopes and compare them with three perturbers inferred through gravitational imaging in PJ011646, SDSS J0946+1006, and JVAS B1938+666. For SIDM model parameters $σ_0/m_χ=147.1$ cm$^2$/g and $w=120$ km/s, SIDM subhalos reproduce all three perturbers more often than CDM subhalos. For PJ011646, we find ~0.6 cored SIDM subhalos per host matching the perturber, compared with ~0.002 in CDM, while core-collapsed subhalos are too steep. For SDSS J0946+1006, we find ~3 core-collapsed and ~0.004 cored SIDM subhalos per host, compared with none in 900 CDM realizations, although baryons, neglected here, may matter for such massive subhalos. For "detection V" in JVAS B1938+666, we find ~220 core-collapsed and ~20 cored SIDM subhalos per host within the $2σ$ posterior region, compared with ~0.2 in CDM; the CDM candidates require exceptionally early accretion, at median redshift $z\sim13$. Simultaneously reproducing all three perturbers requires $w\gtrsim10^2$ km/s, so that the massive (~$5.6\times10^{10}M_\odot$) progenitors of SDSS J0946+1006 candidates can collapse, and is achieved for $σ_0/m_χ\gtrsim10^2$ cm$^2$/g in the parameter sets studied. Our results show how semi-analytic models can quantify how often subhalos reproduce individual perturbers in different dark matter models, and our modular framework can be readily updated as models of tidal stripping and late-stage gravothermal evolution in SIDM improve. (abridged)

title: Physics Informed Neural Network for Multi-dimensional Turbulent Self-gravitating Flows
summary: Molecular clouds exhibit complex, multi-scale dynamics driven by the interplay of turbulence, self-gravity, and gas pressure. Modelling these systems with conventional grid-based methods becomes increasingly expensive as spatial resolution and dimensionality increase. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) offer a mesh-free alternative by incorporating the governing equations directly into the training objective, but their ability to model realistic turbulent self-gravitating flows remains largely unexplored. We apply PINNs to isothermal molecular clouds initialized with astrophysically motivated turbulent velocity fields, considering subsonic and supersonic evolution in two and three dimensions. We benchmark the predicted density and velocity fields against the finite-volume code Athena++. PINNs accurately recover the global evolution of the flow over multiple free-fall times across turbulent realizations, Mach numbers, and dimensionalities. Their training cost also exhibits weak dependence on spatial resolution, increasing by less than 25% from 128^3 to 1024^3 in our experiments. These results demonstrate that PINNs can model substantially more realistic self-gravitating turbulent flows than previously explored and provide a promising complementary framework for studying these systems.

title: Tilt, warp, and dissipation flare in hydrodynamic disks around kicked compact objects
summary: We study the dynamical response of a hydrodynamic disk to an impulsive kick imparted to a central massive object, focusing on the global properties of the material that remains gravitationally bound. We construct a simple analytic model and show that the bound material can acquire a significant tilt---or even a retrograde rotation---if the kick is directed close to the disk midplane. We perform 3D numerical simulations and show that (1) the bound material relaxes to a torus-like circularized flow of which total mass and angular momentum is in fair agreement with the analytic estimate, and (2) in spite of nonlinear hydrodynamic effects, a highly tilted or retrograde disk can be sufficiently formed. The simulations additionally reveal a transient warp in the kicked disk, suggesting a kick as a formation mechanism of tilted or warped disks around compact objects. About 10% of the kinetic energy the bound material acquired from the kick is converted to the internal energy, while the exact conversion efficiency depends on the kick angle and the initial surface mass density profile. The luminosity of this kick-driven dissipation flare can reach $\sim 10^{43}\,{\rm erg\,s^{-1}}$ for strong kicks ($V_{\rm kick} \sim 1000$km/s). We discuss the implications of our results for recoiling supermassive black holes, recoiled stellar-mass black holes in the disks of active galactic nuclei, and natal kicks on compact objects.

title: The SDSS-V Local Volume Mapper (LVM): Technical Overview
summary: The Sloan Digital Sky Survey V (SDSS-V) Local Volume Mapper (LVM) is an ultra-wide integral field spectroscopic survey of the Milky Way, the Magellanic Clouds, and a sample of galaxies in the local volume. The LVM spatially resolved spectroscopy covers the bulk of the optical range (3600-9800 A) at medium spectral-resolution (R = 2200-5500), and maps the disks of these galaxies at high physical spatial resolution (< 1 pc in the MW and ~10 pc in the Magellanic Clouds). Observations are carried out with the LVM Instrument (LVM-I), a custom-built robotic telescope, instrument, and facility located at Las Campanas Observatory (LCO) in Chile. In this article we present a technical overview of the LVM project. We describe the hardware, the survey observing strategy, and the details of how science and calibration observations are carried out. We provide a high-level overview of the survey data flow, including the reduction and calibration of the LVM spectra, and the production of the main data products that are released by the project. We also present an assessment of the LVM data quality and instrumental stability based on science observations. The main goal of this article is to serve as a primer for LVM users, providing the technical information required for the adequate analysis, modeling, and interpretation of the LVM data.

title: Listening to the Standard Candles: A Survey-Scale Search for Phase-Coded Beacons in Cepheids, RR~Lyrae and $β$~Cephei Stars
summary: Learned et al. (2008) proposed that a civilization could use Cepheids and RR Lyrae stars, the most closely watched clocks in astronomy, as beacons, firing pulsations early with a particle beam to write a message into the timing residuals. The one search to date examined a single Kepler star. We describe Star SETI, an automated pipeline that selects Cepheids, RR Lyrae and $β$ Cephei stars from Gaia DR3, measures per-cycle (TESS, Kepler) or block-averaged (ASAS-SN, ZTF) observed-minus-computed timing residuals, tests them for non-white structure, decodes them as a bit stream under the cumulative (``staircase'') modulation of a one-sided trigger, and matches the words to catalogs of recognizable sequences. A resonant antineutrino beam grazing the base of the driving zone needs hundreds to tens of thousands of times less power than a central beam, and driving an RR Lyrae star takes most of its light. Injections into real light curves show that only RR Lyrae stars are detectable near the amplitude that Learned et al. proposed, with half of the codes recovered at 0.2--0.4 per cent of a period per bit in TESS; the ground-based surveys detect only codes held for tens of cycles per bit and decode none. We time 97,725 light curves of 77,596 stars and vet 38,230 timing anomalies; 6823 have timing structure that the vetting cannot attribute to a known cause, all but eight of them on block-averaged timing to which only part of the vetting applies. The highest-ranked are non-radial modes in first-overtone RR Lyrae stars, Blazhko modulation and mode beating in $β$ Cephei stars, and no decoded word survives a false-discovery correction. We find no beacon. That bounds only beacons: a perfectly compressed message is indistinguishable from noise, so a civilization communicating efficiently rather than advertising could leave residuals that pass all of our tests, in stars that we cannot single out.

title: Cluster connectivity in DES Y3 data: impact on galaxy properties
summary: Connectivity, namely the number of cosmic filaments reaching out of groups or clusters, has recently emerged as an informative way to quantify environment. With the advent of wide-area photometric surveys, it becomes possible to measure connectivity on a statistically significant sample of clusters. In this work, we extract the cosmic web from the DES Y3 photometric data and measure the connectivity around clusters from several public catalogs up to $z < 1$. Cosmic filaments are extracted in 2D with DisPerSE (the parametrization of which is calibrated on simulations) in tomographic slices of fixed comoving thickness of 220 Mpc, with a constant sampling across the redshift range ($\sim 0.1$ galaxies Mpc$^{-2}$). We first recover the well-established trend that cluster connectivity increases with cluster mass at all redshifts. We then investigate the properties of cluster member galaxies and find that, at fixed mass, clusters with a higher fraction of red (elliptical) galaxies are more strongly connected to the cosmic web. Furthermore, by examining the radial profiles of the red and elliptical galaxy fractions, we obtain hints that galaxy populations may undergo pre-processing within filamentary structures before being accreted into clusters. Overall, we demonstrate that despite photometric redshift uncertainties and projection effects, our method allows for the quantification of the cosmic web environment around clusters in broad-band photometric surveys. This work is consistent with results based on the Euclid Quick Release 1 (Q1). We plan to publicly release the cluster connectivity catalog as well as the cosmic filament catalog.

title: The Impact of Orbital Data Centers on the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory
summary: As the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory begins its Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), satellite operators are racing to launch Orbital Data Center (ODC) satellites into low-Earth orbit. We present an impact assessment of a simulated $\sim$1 million ODC satellite constellation, arranged per recent filings across two low-Earth and two Sun-synchronous orbit regimes, on one year of Rubin Observatory LSST observations. Our six-stage sequential pipeline combines orbit propagation, field-of-view matching, observer-frame geometry, brightness modeling, surface-brightness calculations, and pixel-loss estimates. We find that on a given night, up to 80% of LSST pointings would contain at least one illuminated ODC satellite streak, depending on the time of year. The yearly average of contaminated exposures is closer to 20%, due to seasonal visibility variations and bright satellite streaks being most prominent near twilight. Sun-synchronous ODCs disproportionately contaminate due to preferential illumination geometry. The ODC satellite brightness distribution is multi-modal, where solar panel specular reflection can appear as bright as 2-4 AB mag ($μ_g \approx 9-11$ mag arcsec$^{-2}$), while diffuse reflections more typically reach 6 AB mag ($μ_g \approx 13-14$ mag arcsec$^{-2}$). Even at 10% deployment, the constellation would still produce widespread visible streak contamination throughout the year. ODC satellites would also drastically increase sky brightness -- by more than 1000% near twilight with no Moon. Launching and operating ODC satellites at this scale would significantly harm LSST science, including typical 5-10% nightly mean pixel losses near twilight, even if multiple mitigation strategies are implemented.

title: Prospects of Detecting Cosmological Domain Walls in the Cosmic Microwave Background
summary: Topological defects are a generic prediction of field theories with spontaneously broken symmetries, and domain walls, the two-dimensional defects left by a broken discrete symmetry, are among the simplest. We study the imprint of dark, purely gravitationally interacting domain walls on the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB), in the regime where a low symmetry-breaking scale $η$ allows the walls to evade the Zel'dovich overclosure bound while remaining cosmologically relevant. The relativistic repulsion of matter by a planar wall carves out an evacuated void bounded by an overdense shell, and we compute the resulting photon deflection field analytically for walls both aligned with and arbitrarily inclined to the line of sight. The deflection stamps coherent, strongly non-Gaussian distortions onto the temperature sky, with a characteristic two-peak structure set by the relativistic displacement scale and an inclination dependence that vanishes for face-on walls. Because these signatures are localised and anisotropic, they are poorly captured by two-point statistics; we therefore analyse them with a curvelet/wavelet decomposition matched to the wall's geometry, and with simulation-based inference, training a Neural Posterior Estimator (NPE) to recover the scattering redshift $z$, energy scale $η$, and inclination $θ$, and a Neural Ratio Estimator (NRE) to evaluate the likelihood-ratio test statistic for limit-setting. Casting these methods as sensitivity forecasts for a South Pole Telescope-like (SPT) survey, we find that the curvelet and wavelet statistical thresholds populate a common $η\sim 10-100$ MeV band over the accessible redshift range.
